precepts.text: Ye that love the Lord, hate evil. In order for the Lord to deliver us out of the hands of the wicked, we must train ourselves to hate evil. As long as you watch pornography, you don't hate evil. You might say it on the street, but at home you don't hate evil.
precepts.point: And when he could not overcome Onias, he got him to Apollonius the governor of Coelosyria and Phenice. He ran to the other nations. They were working together on this temple, and because of one argument he goes to the other nations against Onias, and told them that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money. You cannot make this stuff up.
precepts.why:
Jerusalem was at peace and “the laws were kept very well, because of the godliness of Onias the high priest, and his hatred of wickedness.” That is the mentality we all must have. David says it: “Ye that love the Lord, hate evil: he preserveth the souls of his saints; he delivereth them out of the hand of the wicked.”

In order for the Lord to deliver us out of the hands of the wicked, we must begin to train ourselves to hate evil. A lot of you say you hate evil, but as long as you watch pornography, you don't hate evil. As long as you watch the black woman twerking up and down, you don't hate evil. You might go on the street and say you hate evil, but at home you don't.

Onias hated wickedness, and the whole city benefited. His faith, his strength and his love for God's laws inspired everybody else, so that even the kings honored the place and magnified the temple with their best gifts, and Seleucus paid for the sacrifices out of his own revenues. Your faith helps other people's faith.

That is the promise in the psalm: the Lord preserves the souls of the saints who hate evil and delivers them from the wicked. A city led by a man who truly hates evil is kept in peace.

precepts.text: I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside. The work of them that turn aside is brothers and sisters that leave the truth. They always say we're still serving God, we still keep the commandments; a year or two later they are back with Easter and Thanksgiving.
precepts.point: And when he could not overcome Onias, he got him to Apollonius the governor of Coelosyria and Phenice. He ran to the other nations. They were working together on this temple, and because of one argument he goes to the other nations against Onias, and told them that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money. You cannot make this stuff up.
precepts.why:
Onias was known for “his hatred of wickedness.” David shows what that hatred looks like: “I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside; it shall not cleave to me.”

The work of them that turn aside is brothers and sisters that leave the truth. When they leave, they always say, we're still serving God, we keep the commandments, I've been in ministry for 35 years. Everybody says that. But when you see them a year from now, or two years, they are not serving the Lord. They are back with Easter, back with Thanksgiving, back beating piñatas.

God says, I hate the work of them that turn aside, and it shall not cleave to me. That is what Simon of the tribe of Benjamin did: he was the governor of the temple, working with the high priest, and he turned aside. Hating that work, and not letting it cling to you, is part of hating wickedness the way Onias did.

precepts.text: No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God. When you turn back, regardless of your great speech, you have taken your hand off the plow. You can try to manipulate his words to justify it all you want.
precepts.point: And when he could not overcome Onias, he got him to Apollonius the governor of Coelosyria and Phenice. He ran to the other nations. They were working together on this temple, and because of one argument he goes to the other nations against Onias, and told them that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money. You cannot make this stuff up.
precepts.why:
Simon of the tribe of Benjamin was the governor of the temple, working alongside Onias. When he “fell out with the high priest” and “could not overcome Onias”, he turned back and ran to the nations. Christ says of that: “No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.”

You put your hand to the plow to do the work. Then you get frustrated with brothers always correcting you because you are doing stupid stuff, and now you are mad, you are going to separate yourself and do your own thing. Simple.

Brothers and sisters, when you turn back, regardless of your great speech, we're still keeping the commandments, you have looked back. You have taken your hand off the plow, and Christ said you are not fit for the kingdom of God. You can try to manipulate his words all you want to justify it, but that is what Christ said.

precepts.text: Every friend saith, I am his friend also: but there is a friend, which is only a friend in name. Is it not a grief unto death, when a companion and friend is turned to an enemy? There is a companion which rejoiceth in the prosperity of a friend, but in the time of trouble will be against him. They had one dispute, and he ran to the other nations and told them about all the money in Jerusalem.
precepts.point: And when he could not overcome Onias, he got him to Apollonius the governor of Coelosyria and Phenice. He ran to the other nations. They were working together on this temple, and because of one argument he goes to the other nations against Onias, and told them that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money. You cannot make this stuff up.
precepts.why:
Simon fell out with Onias, and “when he could not overcome Onias”, he went to Apollonius, the governor of Celosyria and Phenice, and “told him that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money.” They were working together on the temple; they had one dispute; Onias as high priest had the last say, and Simon did not agree. So he ran to the other nations against him. You can't make this stuff up.

Sirach describes that man: “Every friend saith, I am his friend also: but there is a friend, which is only a friend in name. Is it not a grief unto death, when a companion and friend is turned to an enemy? O wicked imagination, whence camest thou in to cover the earth with deceit? There is a companion, which rejoiceth in the prosperity of a friend, but in the time of trouble will be against him.”

That is Simon: a friend only in name, a companion turned into an enemy. Because of one argument, he told the heathen about all the money in Jerusalem.

And that money was not his to give away. The treasury held what the law set aside: the tithe for the Levites, who had no inheritance, and for the stranger, the fatherless and the widow, so that the Lord might bless the work of their hands. So he was ready to see the Greeks take what belonged to the widows and orphans rather than let Onias have the last word. This is a no good dude: from brother to betrayer.

precepts.text: The temple had money for widows, so why did the Grecians murmur that their widows were neglected? Because these were followers of Christ, and the priesthood had already agreed to cast out any man who confessed him. So the twelve said, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom. Serving tables means taking care of the widows and orphans; this is how the deacons were chosen, and Stephen was one of the first deacons.
precepts.point: The high priest told him that there was such money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children, and that some of it belonged to Hircanus son of Tobias, a man of great dignity, and not as that wicked Simon had misinformed: in all four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold. And that it was altogether impossible that such wrong should be done unto them that had committed it to the holiness of the place.
precepts.why:
The high priest Onias told Heliodorus “that there was such money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children.” The temple had money in it for the widows. So how come, in the days of the apostles, “there arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration”? Why didn’t they just get it from the temple?

Because these were followers of Christ, and the priesthood had already agreed to cast out any man who confessed him. The widows of the disciples were getting nothing from the temple because they believed in Christ.

So the twelve said, “It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables.” To serve tables means to take care of the widows, the orphans and all of that. “Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business. But we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word.”

This is how the deacons were chosen. “And the saying pleased the whole multitude: and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolas a proselyte of Antioch.” Stephen, the one we always read about, was one of the first deacons chosen. They set them before the apostles, “and when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them.”

So the care of widows and the fatherless has always been a sacred charge among our people, kept in the temple in Onias’s day and put into the deacons’ hands in the apostles’ day. That is what Simon betrayed to the Greeks.

precepts.text: The Jews had agreed already, that if any man did confess that he was Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue. They were kicking people out left and right.
precepts.point: The high priest told him that there was such money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children, and that some of it belonged to Hircanus son of Tobias, a man of great dignity, and not as that wicked Simon had misinformed: in all four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold. And that it was altogether impossible that such wrong should be done unto them that had committed it to the holiness of the place.
precepts.why:
The temple kept money “laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children”, yet in Acts 6 the widows of the disciples were neglected in the daily ministration. Why couldn’t they get it from the temple? John shows what the priesthood had already decided.

The man born blind was healed, and his parents would not answer plainly: “These words spake his parents, because they feared the Jews: for the Jews had agreed already, that if any man did confess that he was Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue.”

They were kicking people out left and right. So Peter and them saw that the widows were not getting anything from the temple, because they believed in Christ. Put out of the synagogue, they were cut off from the relief the temple held for widows and the fatherless.

That is why the apostles had to look out seven men of honest report to serve tables and take care of the widows themselves. And that is how the deacons came to be chosen.

precepts.text: This is how they gauged choosing the seven: the deacons must be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre, and first be proved. And even so must their wives be grave, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things. You didn't just look at the man; you looked at his wife too. If your wife is low down and no good, that is a reflection on you, brother.
precepts.point: The high priest told him that there was such money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children, and that some of it belonged to Hircanus son of Tobias, a man of great dignity, and not as that wicked Simon had misinformed: in all four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold. And that it was altogether impossible that such wrong should be done unto them that had committed it to the holiness of the place.
precepts.why:
The apostles said, look out “seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom”, to take care of the widows. You may ask, what did they base choosing these men on? Timothy shows how they gauged it.

“Likewise must the deacons be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre; Holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless.”

Then: “Even so must their wives be grave, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things. Let the deacons be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well.” You didn’t just look at the man; you looked at his wife too. Sometimes you find a brother who appears decent, but his wife is ratchet, low down, no damn good. That’s a reflection on you, brother. If your wife is low down and no good, you ain’t guiding her right.

So they looked at the man, then they looked at the wife, and said, he has wisdom, he is of honest report, and they chose seven. The ones trusted with what belongs to the widows and the fatherless had to be proved and blameless, the very opposite of a man like Simon, a betrayer of the money.

precepts.text: Honour widows that are widows indeed. A widow indeed had a duty: she trusted in God and continued in supplications and prayers night and day. There was a widowhood of sisters whose job was to pray for Israel, fasting and praying night and day; she didn't just sit around because her husband died. Not under threescore years old, the wife of one man, well reported of for good works. But the younger widows refuse: when they have begun to wax wanton against Christ, they will marry, having damnation, because they have cast off their first faith; that vow was not taken lightly. Let the younger women marry, bear children, guide the house. And if any that believeth have widows in the family, let them relieve them, and let not the church be charged, so the church may relieve them that are widows indeed.
precepts.point: The high priest told him that there was such money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children, and that some of it belonged to Hircanus son of Tobias, a man of great dignity, and not as that wicked Simon had misinformed: in all four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold. And that it was altogether impossible that such wrong should be done unto them that had committed it to the holiness of the place.
precepts.why:
The money in the temple was “laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children.” What is a widow? You may say, a sister whose husband died. But Paul says, “Honour widows that are widows indeed.”

First, “if any widow have children or nephews, let them learn first to shew piety at home, and to requite their parents.” Then: “Now she that is a widow indeed, and desolate, trusteth in God, and continueth in supplications and prayers night and day.” A widow had a duty. “But she that liveth in pleasure is dead while she liveth”, because the widows made a kind of vow to dedicate themselves to the Lord and pray night and day for the benefit of Israel. And “if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel”: the family looks after her first and foremost.

“Let not a widow be taken into the number under threescore years old, having been the wife of one man.” There was a widowhood of sisters whose job was to pray for Israel, fasting and praying night and day. She didn’t just sit around and say, my husband died, I’m a widow. She had an obligation. She had to be sixty, married to one man in her life, “Well reported of for good works”: she raised children, lodged strangers, the brothers who came to the city, washed the saints’ feet, relieved the afflicted.

“But the younger widows refuse: for when they have begun to wax wanton against Christ, they will marry.” Wanton means lustful. She gave up the vow to pray and fast night and day because she wanted a man. “Having damnation, because they have cast off their first faith.” That widowhood was not taken lightly. And they learn to be idle, “wandering about from house to house”, tattlers and busybodies. So “I will therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, guide the house”: get a husband, sister.

“If any man or woman that believeth have widows, let them relieve them, and let not the church be charged; that it may relieve them that are widows indeed.” You, her son, her daughter, her uncle, her brother, take care of her, so the church can care for the real widows who have no family. That is who the money Simon betrayed was for.

precepts.text: An example: Anna, a prophetess, of the tribe of Aser, a widow of about fourscore and four years, which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day.
precepts.point: The high priest told him that there was such money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children, and that some of it belonged to Hircanus son of Tobias, a man of great dignity, and not as that wicked Simon had misinformed: in all four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold. And that it was altogether impossible that such wrong should be done unto them that had committed it to the holiness of the place.
precepts.why:
Paul says a widow indeed “trusteth in God, and continueth in supplications and prayers night and day.” Luke gives an example of exactly that.

“And there was one Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser: she was of a great age, and had lived with an husband seven years from her virginity; And she was a widow of about fourscore and four years, which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day.”

She did not depart from the temple. She served God with fastings and prayers, night and day. That is what widows did. She was married to one man, well over threescore years old, and she gave her life to prayer for Israel.

Those were the widows the temple money was laid up to relieve in Onias’s day: sisters who had dedicated themselves to the Lord. To betray that money to the Greeks was to take the bread from women like Anna.

precepts.text: The bread of the needy is their life: he that defraudeth him thereof is a man of blood; he that taketh away his neighbour's living slayeth him. What Simon did was no light thing. Taking money from the widows, the orphans, the fatherless, and the strangers is murder; that was their livelihood. That is why it is never just one sin.
precepts.point: The high priest told him that there was such money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children, and that some of it belonged to Hircanus son of Tobias, a man of great dignity, and not as that wicked Simon had misinformed: in all four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold. And that it was altogether impossible that such wrong should be done unto them that had committed it to the holiness of the place.
precepts.why:
Onias said there was money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children, “and not as that wicked Simon had misinformed”, and that it was “altogether impossible that such wrongs should be done unto them, that had committed it to the holiness of the place.”

There is a scripture that says keeping a man’s earnings from him is like murder: “The bread of the needy is their life: he that defraudeth him thereof is a man of blood. He that taketh away his neighbour’s living slayeth him; and he that defraudeth the labourer of his hire is a bloodshedder.”

What Simon did was no light thing. Taking money from the widows, the orphans, the fatherless and the strangers is murder. That was their livelihood; we took care of them with that money. Simon would rather have Esau come and take it all than help his own people. He is a murderer.

That is why it is never just one sin. All I did was tell them about the money? No, you did worse than you think. Sin is a domino effect: one hits the next and it goes all around. That is why Onias was in such agony, the priests lay on their faces before the altar and the whole city cried to heaven, and why the Lord of spirits sent the horse with the terrible rider and the two young men to scourge Heliodorus.

precepts.text: The Most High caused a great apparition and sent a rider and two mighty young men who scourged Heliodorus continually when he came to rob the treasury.
precepts.point: When it says He shall send from heaven and save me, look at the history of Heliodorus, who came to take all the funds out of the temple true to the nature of Edom the grape gatherer, and the Most High sent two angels to give the heathen a righteous beating.
precepts.why:
“He shall send from heaven, and save me from the reproach of him that would swallow me up.” Look at the history of Heliodorus, who came to take all the funds out of the temple, true to the nature of Edom the grape gatherer. “Now as he was there present himself with his guard about the treasury, the Lord of spirits, and the Prince of all power, caused a great apparition, so that all that presumed to come in with him were astonished at the power of God, and fainted, and were sore afraid.”

“For there appeared unto them an horse with a terrible rider upon him, and adorned with a very fair covering, and he ran fiercely, and smote at Heliodorus with his forefeet”. Then “two other young men appeared before him, notable in strength, excellent in beauty, and comely in apparel, who stood by him on either side; and scourged him continually, and gave him many sore stripes.” The Most High sent two angels to give the heathen a righteous beating. That is what it looks like when he sends from heaven and saves from the one who would swallow you up.

precepts.text: Seeing thou hast been scourged from heaven, declare unto all men the mighty power of God.
precepts.point: When it says He shall send from heaven and save me, look at the history of Heliodorus, who came to take all the funds out of the temple true to the nature of Edom the grape gatherer, and the Most High sent two angels to give the heathen a righteous beating.
precepts.why: When Heliodorus was scourged, the young men told him: “seeing that thou hast been scourged from heaven, declare unto all men the mighty power of God. And when they had spoken these words, they appeared no more.” Scourged from heaven: that is the Most High sending from heaven to save his people from the reproach of the heathen who came to rob the treasury. Heliodorus had to declare the mighty power of God to all men, and God sent forth his mercy and his truth to his people.

precepts.text: A small example of the greediness of the gang, how Simon informed on the treasury in Jerusalem so it could be brought into the king's hand.
precepts.point: In his estate stands up a vile person to whom they do not give the honor of the kingdom, but he comes in peaceably and obtains the kingdom by flatteries.

note.label: Daniel 11: The Kings of the North and the South

precepts.why:
The vile person obtains the kingdom by flatteries, and Maccabees gives a small example of the greediness of the gang. “one Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, who was made governor of the temple, fell out with the high priest about disorder in the city.” When he could not overcome Onias, he went to Apollonius the son of Thraseas, the governor of Celosyria and Phenice, “And told him that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money, so that the multitude of their riches, which did not pertain to the account of the sacrifices, was innumerable, and that it was possible to bring all into the king’s hand.”

Simon informed on the treasury in Jerusalem so it could be brought into the king's hand. That is the greed at work in the kingdom that comes in peaceably and is obtained by flatteries.

precepts.text: Money was laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children.
precepts.point: Paul sets the age at sixty because younger widows still have fleshly desires and will begin to wax wanton against Christ and want to marry, turning their focus off the work. A woman whose desire is toward the ministry and who has a pattern of good works is worthy to be taken care of; one still looking for a husband should marry and be provided for by a husband.

note.label: Acts 6: The Grecians Were Greek-Speaking Israelites

precepts.why:
The relief of widows was an old practice of the temple: “Then the high priest told him that there was such money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children”.

Money was laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children. The daily ministration in Acts 6 is that same care carried on in the church, and the murmuring arose because the widows of the Grecians, the Israelites of the Greek captivity, were being neglected in it.

points: The holy city was inhabited with all peace, and the laws were kept very well, because of the godliness of Onias the high priest and his hatred of wickedness. Because of Onias's faith, his strength and love for God's laws, that inspired everybody else; even the kings themselves honored the place and magnified the temple with their best gifts. Seleucus king of Asia, of the line of Alexander's four generals (Lysimachus over Thrace and Asia Minor, Cassander over Macedonia and Greece, Ptolemy over Egypt, Seleucus over Babylon and Syria), bore all the costs of the sacrifices out of his own revenues.

But one Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, who was made governor of the temple, fell out with the high priest about disorder in the city. The role of the temple governor was read: management of temple resources, maintenance of the temple, administration of worship, handling disputes, coordination with other authorities, and security. Whatever the dispute was, Onias as high priest had the last say.

And when he could not overcome Onias, he got him to Apollonius the governor of Coelosyria and Phenice. He ran to the other nations. They were working together on this temple, and because of one argument he goes to the other nations against Onias, and told them that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money. You cannot make this stuff up.

Apollonius told the king of the money, and the king chose Heliodorus his treasurer and sent him to bring the money. Heliodorus took his journey under a colour of visiting the cities of Coelosyria and Phenice, but indeed to fulfil the king's purpose: that is what he let everybody think he was doing.

The high priest told him that there was such money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children, and that some of it belonged to Hircanus son of Tobias, a man of great dignity, and not as that wicked Simon had misinformed: in all four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold. And that it was altogether impossible that such wrong should be done unto them that had committed it to the holiness of the place.

Before that, the priests prostrated themselves before the altar in their vestments and called unto heaven; the women girt with sackcloth abounded in the streets, the virgins ran to the gates and walls, and all held their hands toward heaven. Whoso had looked the high priest in the face, it would have wounded his heart; Onias was in agony because he knew that taking that money would affect the widows and orphans of Jerusalem.

Heliodorus executed that which was decreed; but as he was there with his guard about the treasury, the Lord of spirits caused a great apparition: a horse with a terrible rider smote at Heliodorus with his forefeet, and two young men, notable in strength, excellent in beauty, scourged him continually. He fell to the ground compassed with great darkness, and they carried him out, unable to help himself with his weapons; manifestly they acknowledged the power of God.

Heliodorus's friends begged Onias to call upon the Most High to grant him his life. The high priest, suspecting lest the king should think some treachery had been done to Heliodorus by the Jews, offered a sacrifice for the health of the man. The same young men appeared and said, give Onias the high priest great thanks, insomuch as for his sake the Lord hath granted thee life; and seeing that thou hast been scourged from heaven, declare unto all men the mighty power of God.
